content: Hepatitis B vaccination is the most effective method to prevent infection with the hepatitis B virus (HBV) and its associated complications, including liver cirrhosis, liver cancer, liver failure, and death. In adults, ongoing HBV transmission primarily occurs among unvaccinated individuals with behavioral risk factors for HBV transmission, such as heterosexuals with multiple sexual partners, injection drug users, and men who have sex with men. It also occurs among household contacts and sexual partners of individuals with chronic HBV infection. This report, the second part of a two-part statement from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), provides updated recommendations to increase hepatitis B vaccination among adults at risk for HBV infection. The first part of the ACIP statement, which focused on immunization recommendations for infants, children, and adolescents, was published previously. HBV can lead to chronic infection, resulting in liver cirrhosis, liver cancer, liver failure, and death. Individuals with chronic HBV infection serve as the primary reservoir for continued transmission. Chronic infection is more likely to develop in individuals infected as infants or young children, although new infections and acute disease are most common among adults. Approximately 95% of primary HBV infections in adults with normal immune status are self-limited, with the virus being cleared from the blood and long-lasting immunity developing. Chronic infection occurs in about 5% of infected adults, 30% of infected children under 5 years old, and 90% of infected infants. Hepatitis B vaccination has been successfully integrated into the childhood vaccination schedule, with high coverage rates among infants and adolescents. Universal infant vaccination, prevention of perinatal HBV transmission through routine screening of pregnant women for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), and vaccination of at-risk adults have contributed to a significant decline in acute hepatitis B incidence in the United States. Despite these successes, HBV transmission remains a concern among unvaccinated adults with risk factors, such as those engaging in high-risk sexual behaviors, injection drug use, or living with individuals with chronic HBV infection. Vaccination coverage among adults at risk increased from 30% to 45% between 2000 and 2004, contributing to a 35% decline in acute hepatitis B incidence during this period. However, the incidence of acute hepatitis B remains highest among adults, who accounted for 95% of an estimated 51,000 new HBV infections in 2005. The ACIP recommends universal hepatitis B vaccination for all adults in settings where a high proportion of individuals are at risk for HBV infection, such as sexually transmitted disease (STD) clinics, HIV testing and treatment facilities, drug treatment centers, and correctional facilities. In primary care and specialty medical settings, standing orders should be implemented to identify adults recommended for hepatitis B vaccination and administer the vaccine as part of routine services. HBV is a 42-nm DNA virus classified in the Hepadnaviridae family, with the liver being the primary site of replication. HBV infection can be asymptomatic or symptomatic, with an average incubation period of 90 days. Symptoms, when present, may include anorexia, malaise, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Extrahepatic manifestations, such as skin rashes, arthralgias, and arthritis, can also occur. No specific treatment exists for acute hepatitis B, and supportive care is the mainstay of therapy. Chronic HBV infection requires medical evaluation and regular monitoring. FDA-approved therapeutic agents can achieve sustained suppression of HBV replication and remission of liver disease in some individuals. Periodic screening with ultrasonography and alpha-fetoprotein can enhance early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), improving survival outcomes. HBV is highly stable in the environment and can remain viable on surfaces for over seven days. Transmission can also occur in household settings, particularly among individuals living with someone with chronic HBV infection. The ACIP emphasizes the importance of increasing hepatitis B vaccination coverage among adults, particularly those at risk for infection. This includes providing information about the health benefits of vaccination, assessing individual risk factors, and vaccinating all adults who report risk factors or request protection from HBV infection.
